papers.title: A data-driven approach for learning traffic assignment using an artificial neural network
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Transport
papers.abstract: Solving transportation network design problems using traffic assignment models becomes increasingly impractical as the size of the considered network grows, due to the need to evaluate numerous candidate solutions. This study aims to model the traffic assignment process through a data-driven approach, and introduces a model based on an artificial neural network (ANN) to predict the total travel time in a network under various link capacity modifications for a specified set of links. ANN-based prediction models are trained and validated on a synthetic data set generated from a medium-sized network to evaluate the feasibility of the proposed approach. Models developed using different ANN architectures highlight the importance of selecting the most suitable architecture specific to the problem. The practical value of the ANN-based prediction model becomes apparent when used in optimising a transportation network design problem instead of the traditional traffic-assignment model: the ANN-based model reduced by up to 60 000 times the computation time required for the optimisation.

papers.title: Digital twin in design architecture: Impact of DT in architectural design for improved building lifecycle management
papers.journal: Journal of Information Technology in Construction
papers.abstract: Digital twins (DTs) are increasingly transforming the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) industry by enhancing data integration, visualization, collaboration, and decision-making throughout the building lifecycle. Despite these advances, limited research has examined the role of DTs in supporting architectural design for improved Building Lifecycle Management (BLM), particularly during the early design stages. This study investigates the potential of DT technology to enhance BLM by integrating digital twin concepts into the architectural design process. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a comprehensive literature review with a questionnaire survey of 60 architecture, engineering, and construction professionals from Saudi Arabia, Nigeria, and the United States to evaluate current awareness, perceived benefits, implementation challenges, and opportunities associated with DT adoption. The findings indicate that while awareness of DT technology is increasing, its application to architectural design for comprehensive BLM remains limited. The study identifies key opportunities for improving decision-making, sustainability, lifecycle performance, and stakeholder collaboration, while highlighting workforce skills, interoperability, and implementation complexity as major barriers to adoption. By integrating literature-based evidence with industry perspectives, the research clarifies how design-stage decisions, digital information, and lifecycle requirements can be connected more effectively through DT-enabled processes. The findings further emphasize the importance of early planning for data integration, sensing requirements, performance evaluation, and interdisciplinary coordination. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on digital twin applications in architectural design by providing an evidence-based assessment of current adoption, opportunities, and challenges, offering practical insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to advance Building Lifecycle Management through digital transformation.

papers.title: Design and development of a test bench for railway coupler testing
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part F Journal of Rail and Rapid Transit
papers.abstract: Accurate modelling and experimental characterization of railway coupling devices are essential to reliably estimate the maximum longitudinal compressive and tensile forces to which a trainset is subjected. These estimates are paramount to ensure safe and efficient operations, particularly for longer and heavier freight trains. However, traditional testing of couplers is based on simple, standardized tests which fail to correctly reproduce their behaviour under realistic conditions. Moreover, these methodologies cannot be easily interfaced with numerical simulation tools. This paper presents the design and development of an innovative test bench for the experimental analysis of several types of railway couplers. The test bench can actuate a moving frame with two translational and one rotational degree of freedom in the horizontal plane, allowing indoor reproduction of relative motions between adjacent wagons. The bench is compatible with both conventional buffer-and-hook systems and Digital Automatic Couplers (DACs) and is equipped with a comprehensive measurement system for forces, moments, and displacements. The effects of uncertainties on the measurement setup are also discussed. The capabilities of the test bench are assessed through an experimental campaign on a standard UIC coupling system assembly, including compression and traction tests up to realistic load levels and an open-loop simulation of a trainset negotiating a double switch. The proposed test bench represents a flexible and effective tool for advanced experimental characterization of railway couplers and a solid basis for future Hardware-in-the-Loop based longitudinal dynamics investigations.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence–assisted integration of phase change material-embedded clay bricks for net-zero modular construction
papers.abstract: Purpose This study develops an exploratory artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted framework for integrating phase change material (PCM)-embedded clay bricks into modular wall assemblies to support net-zero building performance. The work addresses the current absence of scalable, climate-adaptive PCM–modular integration strategies and evaluates their potential for energy savings, thermal stability and lifecycle carbon reduction. Design/methodology/approach A multi-scale methodology was adopted, combining EnergyPlus v26.1 building simulations, a representative laboratory thermal-cycling dataset and a hypothetical Toronto case study. PCM-embedded bricks containing 10 wt% microencapsulated paraffin (melting point 24°C) were modeled within modular wall panels. Annual simulations were conducted across diverse Köppen climate zones, including per-zone re-optimization of PCM melting point, loading fraction and wall placement using a Physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate model coupled with a genetic algorithm (GA). A streamlined ISO 14040/44 lifecycle assessment (LCA) estimated embodied carbon, operational savings and carbon payback. AI-assisted outputs are treated as qualitative due to limited empirical validation. Findings Simulations indicate cooling energy savings of approximately 25% ± 5% in temperate climates (London) and up to 30% ± 5% in hot-arid climates (Dubai), with peak indoor temperature reductions of 3–4°C. All energy savings are upper-bound estimates, as PCM thermal hysteresis (1–4°C band, reducing effective storage by 15–30%) was not modeled. Laboratory cycling demonstrated a 66% improvement in thermal stability with no leakage across 100 cycles. The modeled LCA projects an additional 8.8 kg CO2eq/m2 of embodied carbon and an estimated carbon payback of approximately 3.4 years under Toronto conditions. Economic payback was estimated at approximately 10.6 years based on current Toronto electricity pricing. AI-assisted optimization reduced design iteration by approximately 40% compared to conventional parametric sweeps. Originality/value This study is the first to link AI-assisted PCM optimization (PINN surrogate + GA), modular precision manufacturing and PCM-embedded clay bricks within a unified framework for net-zero construction. It advances the field by integrating multi-climate simulation with per-zone parameter re-optimization, a small-scale laboratory cycling dataset (100 cycles), lifecycle modeling with inflation and end-of-life scenarios, and a formal sensitivity analysis, establishing a preliminary pathway toward scalable, low-carbon and climate-adaptive modular building envelopes.

papers.title: Jetted helical anchor installation as a torque reducing technique
papers.abstract: Helical piles and anchors are being increasingly considered for offshore renewable energy applications. However, the very high installation torque required at the scales relevant to offshore use remains a significant barrier to their deployment. This paper investigates a torque-reduction strategy based on water jetting around the helix during installation, which generates excess pore pressure, reduces effective stress and consequently lowers the required installation torque. A series of model scale centrifuge experiments in dense sand examines the influence of jetting flow rate, nozzle configuration, helix size and embedment depth on both the required installation torque and the subsequent uplift capacity. The results demonstrate that jetting leads to a substantial reduction in installation torque, enabling significantly greater embedment depths, larger helix diameters, or a combination of both. While jetting results in a modest reduction in tensile capacity, this effect is more than offset by the much higher capacity achievable through deeper installation under reduced torque demand.

papers.title: Understanding the thermal behaviour of MSWI bottom ash foamed ternary geopolymer: The fundamental role of pore structure
papers.abstract: Porous materials are widely used in refractory applications, but conventional foaming relies on energy-intensive equipment or chemical agents, increasing cost and carbon footprint. Municipal solid waste incineration bottom ash (MSWI BA) provides a low-carbon alternative, as its inherent metallic aluminium can produce foams in the alkali environment. However, uncontrolled gas generation may lead to expansion cracks within the matrix during hardening. In this study, a novel method is proposed to develop a porous Class F fly ash based geopolymer with inhibited crack formation by incorporating steelmaking byproduct ladle slag, which regulates the foaming process induced by MSWI BA. Through adjusting precursors composition, the pore structure is tailored, and systematically characterized to correlate with drying shrinkage, mechanical performance and thermal behaviour. Results indicate that the tortuosity of capillary network is the key factor retarding moisture loss of samples, which in turn affects drying shrinkage, with ultimate values as low as 306 microstrain. Moreover, interconnected macropore structure is found to determine thermal cracking resistance. After 1000 °C exposure, highly connected macropore structure largely maintains the structural integrity of samples, enabling an approximately 200% enhancement in compressive strength relative to room temperature performance. Accordingly, a conceptual model is proposed to understand the influence of pore structure on moisture movement at both ambient and elevated temperatures. This work offers practical insights into waste valorisation and pore structure design, guiding the customization of porous geopolymer to achieve enhanced high temperature performance.

papers.title: Knowledge infusion process and challenges in outbound construction service consultant–supplier interfaces
papers.abstract: Purpose Construction service supply chain (CSSC) networks are known for their substantial interactions and knowledge transfer between consultants and suppliers. However, the knowledge infusion (KI) process and the associated challenges in these networks still receive little research attention, particularly in the context of outbound, dispersed consultant–supplier interfaces. Design/methodology/approach This study explores the phenomenon adopting a convergent mixed-methods design that integrated literature-based inductive and qualitative-deductive approaches. The resulting framework was empirically corroborated using 25 semi-structured interviews with construction service consulting firms and suppliers in Tanzania. Findings Our findings show that KI in outbound consultant supplier interfaces is unevenly enacted across firms and only partially aligns with a systematic process of principled reasoning, robust logics, real time data capture and transactive memory systems. The findings further suggest that the temporary, one off and geographically dispersed nature of these interfaces prevents knowledge from being consistently captured, codified, stored, retrieved and reused. As a result, KI remains largely incidental, unstructured and static, while relational complexity, project interdependencies, knowledge leakage and knowledge inertia further constrain decision quality and service innovation. Originality/value The current literature on KI offers a limited understanding of how the KI process is orchestrated within CSSC networks. Thus, this study proposes a framework for achieving an effective KI process in the context of outbound consultant-supplier interactions. It further highlights theoretical and empirical implications for managers. The study also offers avenues for future research as efforts to address the (KI) challenges in achieving axiomatized knowledge, confidence in decision-making and service innovation performance.

papers.title: Mechanical and structural performance of reinforcement strategies in 3D concrete printing: A review
papers.abstract: Abstract 3D concrete printing (3DCP) has emerged in recent decades as a promising construction technology that minimizes labor‐intensive and time‐consuming processes. Reinforcement integration is essential to ensure structural integrity and durability, particularly for large‐scale applications. While many reviews have focused on reinforcement classifications, there remains a lack of in‐depth evaluation of mechanical and structural performance, automation feasibility, and large‐scale validation. This review addresses these gaps by critically examining three categories of reinforcement: intralayer (fibers, cables, continuous yarns), interlayer (steel rebar, barbed wire, screws), and across‐layer (steel cages, meshes, post‐tensioning). Intralayer reinforcement offers excellent automation compatibility and design freedom, but contributes little to large‐scale load resistance due to discontinuity and low stiffness. Interlayer reinforcement improves bonding and ductility but introduces matrix disturbance and anchorage challenges. Across‐layer reinforcement provides the most reliable structural performance, essential for seismic and load‐bearing capacity, but limited automation maturity and design freedom. Hybrid systems emerge as promising strategies, combining material‐ and structural‐level reinforcement to enhance ductility, toughness, and load capacity, though their integration remains costly, complex, and less automation‐friendly. Current investigations are disproportionately skewed toward flexural behavior, while critical tests such as pull‐out, interlayer bond strength, compression, shear, and seismic loading are underexplored. Future work should prioritize large‐scale/field‐scale and long‐term structural validation, develop standardized fabrication and testing protocols, and advance reinforcement strategies that reconcile automation potential with structural reliability.

papers.title: Feature-knowledge-guided and direction-adaptive recognition of cross-sea bridges from high-spatial-resolution remote sensing imagery
papers.abstract: Cross-sea bridges are critical components of coastal transportation networks, and their accurate recognition is essential for infrastructure mapping, geographic information updating, and emergency assessment. However, reliable recognition from high-spatial-resolution remote sensing imagery remains challenging because of complex coastal backgrounds and the large variation in bridge orientations. This study aims to improve the robustness and directional adaptability of cross-sea bridge recognition while retaining the interpretability and low sample dependence of knowledge-driven approaches. An integrated framework is developed by combining image enhancement, land–sea spatial constraints, bridge-specific feature knowledge, and direction-adaptive mathematical morphology. Water bodies are first extracted to constrain the recognition space, after which local water-connectivity directions are estimated to guide adaptive morphological reconstruction. Candidate bridge regions are then identified and screened using spatial and geometric knowledge. Experiments using GF-2 imagery over the Zhoushan Archipelago show that all four cross-sea bridges with different orientations were successfully identified, with good positional consistency and a maximum bridge-length deviation of 1.54%. The results demonstrate that integrating environmental context, feature knowledge, and directional adaptation provides an interpretable and sample-efficient solution for cross-sea bridge recognition, with potential applications in coastal infrastructure mapping, geographic information updating, and rapid bridge identification.

papers.title: A kinematically-constrained Hankel dynamic mode decomposition for short-term prediction of ship manoeuvring in ambient currents
papers.abstract: The accurate prediction of vessel manoeuvring dynamics is essential for ensuring navigational safety in the transition toward maritime autonomy. In this study, a kinematically-constrained Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel-DMD) approach is developed to model and predict vessel manoeuvring dynamics. The vessel motion is represented using a state formulation consisting of position and resultant speed, and the Hankel-DMD method, together with a component-wise normalisation of the position states, is used to extract the modes governing the system dynamics. To improve the physical consistency of the prediction, a kinematic constraint linking vessel position and speed is incorporated as a post-processing reconstruction step. The developed approach is examined using the data generated from a physics-based Maneuvering Modelling Group (MMG) manoeuvring model for an azimuth thruster-equipped tug. Three cases are considered, including manoeuvring in calm water, in the presence of ambient current along the X -direction (following), and current along the Y -direction (cross). Quantitative error metrics show that the kinematically-constrained reconstruction reduces the trajectory RMSE by 71% in calm water (from 1.09 m to 0.31 m) and by 60% for the following current (from 7.31 m to 2.90 m). For the cross current, however, the XY-normalised pure Hankel-DMD prediction achieves the slightly lower RMSE (1.34 m versus 2.80 m for the constrained reconstruction), indicating that the benefit of the kinematic constraint is scenario-dependent. These findings demonstrate that incorporating a kinematic constraint can improve the robustness of data-driven vessel trajectory prediction, although its benefit is case-dependent under environmental disturbances.

papers.title: Low-cost single-beam SONAR localization in AUVs: Systematic experiments with acoustic and optical perception
papers.abstract: This work presents a low-cost acoustic sensing framework for underwater robot (UWR) localization and perception, using single-beam sonars (SBS) and an external forward-looking sonar (FLS) for confined environments in place of costlier Doppler velocity logs (DVL) and onboard imaging suites. Instead of utilizing an SBS for depth estimation alone, an SBS unit each is also used in surge and sway directions for localization. A Kalman filter fuses sparse SBS measurements with inertial sensing via moving averaging and confidence-based gating, suppressing multi-path and orientation-driven anomalies. SBS-assisted fusion achieves sub-meter accuracy, reducing localization errors by more than 70% versus inertial sensing alone via acoustic corrections comprising just 27% of measurements. To further mitigate potential SBS tracking losses, an FLS is proposed to be deployed on an external parent platform, such that it can independently track multiple UWRs. Parent–child tracking achieves 0.063 m average error when combined with SBS estimates. Stabilized pose estimates anchor optical mosaicking and acoustic point-cloud reconstruction, cutting required image data to about 1% for mosaicking and 5%–25% for point clouds versus unassisted collection. Per-vehicle sensor cost falls to approximately $2000 for a ten-vehicle fleet, an order of magnitude below DVLs and ultra-short baseline alternatives.
